subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Dust Bowl
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Dust Bowl.

hook.text: In the 1930s, the American Great Plains turned to dust. Farms blew away in the wind.

buildup.text: Farmers had plowed up deep-rooted prairie grass, leaving bare soil exposed to the wind.

discovery.text: When drought hit, there was nothing to hold the topsoil. Black blizzards buried entire towns.

twist.text: Dust storms reached New York and Washington, D.C. — darkening skies 2,500 km away.

climax.text: 2.5 million people fled the plains. It was the largest migration in American history.

punchline.text: The land gave everything it had. Then the wind took it.

quiz.question: What human action worsened the Dust Bowl?

details.summary: The Dust Bowl of the 1930s struck the American Great Plains when severe drought combined with decades of poor farming practices that had stripped protective grassland. Massive dust storms darkened skies, destroyed crops, and displaced hundreds of thousands of people.
details.whyItMatters: The Dust Bowl remains the worst ecological disaster in US history. Its lessons about soil conservation and climate vulnerability are directly relevant to modern agricultural challenges.
takeaways: Deep plowing destroyed drought-resistant prairie grass across millions of acres
Massive dust storms carried soil as far as Washington DC and New York
The crisis led to the creation of the Soil Conservation Service

faq.question: Could a Dust Bowl happen again?
faq.answer: Modern soil conservation practices make an exact repeat unlikely, but the Ogallala Aquifer that supports Great Plains farming is being depleted, and climate change is intensifying drought. A severe prolonged drought could still devastate agriculture in the region.

faq.question: How did the Dust Bowl change farming practices?
faq.answer: The federal government created the Soil Conservation Service, promoted contour plowing, windbreaks, and crop rotation, and paid farmers to adopt conservation practices. These reforms dramatically reduced erosion, though some have eroded over time.
